channel.title: Runway Briefing
channel.description: Your daily five-minute briefing on the aviation industry — new routes, airline strategy, fleet orders, and the moves shaping how we fly. Delivered daily like a friend catching you up over coffee.
channel.itunes:author: Runway Briefing

item.title: Weekly Deep Dive: AirBaltic's Bankruptcy and the A220's Reckoning
item.description: AirBaltic just filed for Chapter 11, and it's not just a Latvian airline's problem — it's a stress test for the entire A220 program and the idea that betting your whole airline on one aircraft type is a smart strategy. Ryan and Hope dig into what actually broke at airBaltic, why the engines are the real villain of this story, and what it means for every other airline that's ordered hundreds of these jets.

item.title: Amazon's Deadly Miami Crash: Cargo Aviation's Safety Blind Spot
item.description: A Prime Air-branded Boeing 767 freighter overran the runway in Miami and killed at least five people, and this week we go deep on why cargo aviation operates under a completely different safety rulebook than the passenger airlines you fly. We trace the eerie parallels to the 2019 Atlas Air crash, explain why cargo pilots are exempt from fatigue rules that apply to everyone else, and ask whether Amazon's breakneck expansion is outrunning its safety culture.

item.title: Boeing's Engineers Could Ground the 777X, Delta's Very Bad Day With a Casket, and United's Polaris Lounges Can't Keep Up
item.description: Boeing's engineers might walk out October 6th, and that could freeze the already-years-late 777X right when it needs to get certified. Plus, a heartbreaking story about Delta mishandling a family's loss, United's new 787s are so popular in business class that the lounges can't handle the crowd, and Finnair is about to fly one of the longest scheduled routes in the world.

item.title: Runway Briefing: Missile Strike Shuts Down Riyadh, Ukraine's Drone War Grounds Russian Airports, and American Finally Fixes Its Delay Lies
item.description: A Houthi missile slips past Saudi defenses and hits a fuel depot at Riyadh's main airport, and it's part of a bigger pattern of war zones rewriting flight maps. Plus, US airlines fight to keep China's carriers grounded, American finally admits rolling delays are a scam, and a fuel truck at JFK does some very expensive damage to an Air China 747.

item.title: KLM's Ex-CEO Sets Business Class on Fire, Delta Piles Into LAX, and AirAsia Says It's Fine, Actually
item.description: A former KLM CEO becomes the star of his own airline's power bank nightmare somewhere over the Atlantic. Plus, Delta goes all in on Los Angeles with its biggest schedule ever, AirAsia insists it's not collapsing despite the government quietly lining up a backup plan, and a private jet broker sits on $150 million of your money while it "reviews things."

item.title: Fuel Prices Force Airline Cutbacks, American's Basic Economy Backfires, and Etihad's A380 Finally Comes Home
item.description: Fuel prices spike thanks to the Iran situation, and suddenly American, United, and Southwest are all quietly cutting flights instead of adding them. Plus, American admits it may have gone too far with Basic Economy, Etihad finally reactivates its last grounded A380 after six and a half years, and yes, we have to talk about the dog on the Southwest flight.

item.title: American's XLR Seats Keep Breaking, Delta Quietly Cuts 21 Cities, and Qatar Backs Off Its Avios Crackdown
item.description: American's shiny new A321XLRs have a business class problem — the seats keep getting stuck. Plus, Delta's been trimming long-haul cities you probably didn't notice, Breeze pilots call in a federal mediator, and Qatar Airways quietly walks back one of the more annoying loyalty changes we've covered this year.

item.title: Chicago's Airline Turf War Heats Up, JFK's Terminal One Slips Again, and Congress Wants to Gut National Airport
item.description: American is literally handing out free elite status on planes to keep Chicago flyers loyal, while United counters with a Tokyo route relaunch — welcome to the hottest hub fight in the country. Plus, JFK's shiny new Terminal One pushes to 2027 (even as Air France unveils a massive new lounge for it), a Senate bill could gut half of Reagan National's long-haul flights, and new NTSB data reveals exactly what went wrong on that Amazon cargo jet in Miami.

item.title: airBaltic Files Chapter 11, American Eyes Singapore Again, and a Cargo Plane's Owner Gets the Boot
item.description: Latvia's flag carrier heads to a New York bankruptcy court while insisting flights keep flying — turns out betting big on a single aircraft type has a dark side too. Plus, American Airlines might return to a route it once ran away from, Amazon cuts ties with the cargo airline behind last week's Miami runway overrun, and a shouting match on the tarmac in Atlanta raises real questions about who actually has the final word before takeoff.

item.title: LaGuardia's Missing Controllers, Virgin Atlantic's Route Cuts, and Frontier's Oakland Gamble
item.description: New details emerge about the LaGuardia tower on the night an Air Canada CRJ hit a fire truck on the runway, and it's not a good look for the FAA. Plus, Virgin Atlantic quietly guts its long-haul map, Frontier sniffs out opportunity in Oakland now that Southwest's pulled back, and a Denver airport breakup goes about as well as you'd expect.

item.title: United's Orphaned Seats, Ryanair Clips a Wingtip in Dublin, and the Sonic Boom Ban Might Be Ending
item.description: United has hundreds of business class seats sitting in storage for a plane it still can't fly, and the story is somehow both hilarious and expensive. Plus, a Ryanair 737 MAX scrapes a wingtip aborting a landing in Dublin crosswinds, the FAA quietly moves to end the 53-year ban on supersonic flight over the US, and Nashville's airport might soon be named after Dolly Parton.

item.title: 25 Years Since 9/11, Emirates Finally Gets Berlin, and JetBlue Hits Pause on Growth
item.description: It's the 25th anniversary of 9/11, and we look at how the day still shapes everything from cockpit doors to TSA water bottle rules — plus a wild story about a Korean Air 747 almost getting shot down hours after the attacks. Also today: Emirates wins its Berlin fight while Algeria slams its airspace shut on UAE carriers, and JetBlue quietly pushes 44 new jets off into the future.

item.title: NTSB's Grim Amazon Update, United Cancels Its Own 9/11 Flypast, and Hyatt Ditches American for Delta
item.description: The NTSB drops new cockpit voice data from Sunday's fatal Miami crash, and it's about as bad as you'd expect. United quietly scraps a bizarre 9/11 tribute flight over Denver, Hyatt swaps American for Delta as its loyalty partner, and Frontier finally heads to South America. Plus, Air Canada's shiny new A321XLR already flopped on its biggest route.

item.title: Amazon's 767 Crash Gets Grimmer, London Grinds to a Halt, and Delta Quietly Shrinks Vegas
item.description: The NTSB drops new flight data from Sunday's fatal Amazon cargo crash in Miami, and it raises more questions than it answers. Heathrow and the rest of London's airports basically shut down after an air traffic control glitch, Delta trims five routes heading into winter, and American and Hyatt are calling it quits. Plus, GE just wrote an $11.75 billion check to fix a problem that's been grounding planes.

item.title: NTSB Details the Miami Crash, Delta's Scary Descent, and American Kills First Class (Sort Of)
item.description: NTSB briefs reporters on the fatal Prime Air 767 crash we covered yesterday, and it's grim. A Delta 737 makes an emergency dive from 35,000 feet after a depressurization scare over the Mojave. Plus, American Airlines is killing off its actual first class cabin while still honoring $250,000 lifetime passes for it, and Delta keeps quietly abandoning JFK even as Frontier heads for the exit entirely.

item.title: Amazon's Deadly Miami Crash, United Flies Back to Tel Aviv, and a Duct-Taped Passenger Loses His Job
item.description: A cargo 767 overruns the runway in Miami and it's fatal — we break down what we know so far. United beats Delta back into Tel Aviv as Middle East service slowly reopens, and the guy who got duct-taped to his American Airlines seat has now lost his job too. Plus, a preserved A340 goes out in flames and a Southwest bag drop gets someone sued.

item.title: Boeing Tears Open 30 777Xs, American Flirts With The A330neo Right As Its Engine Gets Flagged, and a Drone Shuts Down San Diego
item.description: Boeing's 777X problem gets weirder — finished jets now have to be partially disassembled before they can ever fly a passenger. American Airlines is circling the exact same plane whose engine just got an FAA safety order. Plus, a drone and a weather balloon shut down San Diego for hours, and we cover a genuinely tragic ramp accident in Montreal.

item.title: Qantas Dumps the A380 Early, Virgin Cuts North America, and DOT Lets Airlines Off the Hook for Your Hotel
item.description: Qantas just moved up the retirement of its superjumbo fleet by four years — turns out betting on four engines was a mistake everyone's making now. Plus, Virgin Atlantic quietly axes five long-haul routes to North America, Frontier packs up from JFK after just two years, and a new DOT rule means your broken plane might not get you a hotel room anymore.

item.title: American's Widebody Gamble, Boeing's Air Force One Cracks, and Ukraine Warns the Skies Over Russia Are Closing
item.description: American Airlines is dangling up to 65 widebody jets in front of Airbus after years of retiring planes it probably shouldn't have. Boeing's Air Force One replacement is now getting patched for cracks on top of a $3 billion overrun, and Zelensky just told every airline still flying over Russia that the sky is about to get a lot less friendly. Plus, Emirates finally makes premium economy look like a real cabin instead of an afterthought.

item.title: Air Canada Goes Big, Southwest Gets Lounges, and a Cuba Flight Turns Into a Bomb Joke Nobody Should've Made
item.description: Air Canada just announced its biggest international expansion ever, and Southwest — the airline that used to brag about not having assigned seats — is building actual airport lounges with Chase. Plus, Zelensky tells airlines to stay out of Russian airspace entirely, Delta has a scary pattern with sick pilots, and one passenger in Miami picks the worst possible joke to make at a gate agent.

item.title: American Kills First Class, BA Guts Heathrow, and JetBlue Finally Gets a First Class Cabin
item.description: American Airlines unveils its swanky new Flagship Suites and sets a hard end date for international first class — while somehow also housing delayed passengers in a hotel with the ceiling ripped open. Plus, British Airways slashes 77 routes from Heathrow, JetBlue finally reveals its long-awaited domestic first class, and United's top status tier proves that loyalty, apparently, has a price tag of five million dollars.

item.title: Runway Briefing: United's Stranded Seats, Delta's Hawaii Whiplash, and JetBlue Buys Its Way Into LaGuardia
item.description: United bought hundreds of fancy lie-flat seats for a plane that still doesn't exist, and now they might not even fit. Delta can't decide if it wants to fly to Hawaii or not. Plus, JetBlue pays nearly sixty million bucks for old Spirit slots, and United's new app feature quietly makes life miserable for airline employees flying standby.

item.title: An Independent Reporter Loses His Home, Etihad Bets Big, and United's CEO Wants Chicago All to Himself
item.description: The founder of Aviation Herald, one of the most trusted names in aviation safety reporting, just lost his home fighting a defamation lawsuit for reporting something that turned out to be true. Plus, a Russian smuggling ring gets caught funneling spare parts to sanctioned Aeroflot, Etihad announces a massive $20 billion expansion plan, and United's Scott Kirby has some very convenient thoughts about American's struggles in Chicago.

item.title: Icahn Bails on JetBlue, Everyone's Cutting Routes, and Your Engine Oil Might Be Lying to You
item.description: Carl Icahn dumps his entire JetBlue stake at a loss after his board seats went up in smoke — so was this activist investing or just a really expensive shrug? Plus, Allegiant, Alaska, Frontier, and WestJet all take a hatchet to their fall schedules on the same day, a flight attendant union sounds the alarm on engine oil designed to NOT smell bad, and a Delta flight strands its own passengers after a TSA checkpoint closes for the night.

item.title: Episode Title: Air Canada's A321XLR Face-Plants on London, Delta and United Want to Be Singapore Airlines, and Frontier Guts Elite Status
item.description: Air Canada's shiny new A321XLR couldn't even make it through its debut season on the Toronto-London route before getting yanked. Plus, Delta's Ed Bastian and United's Scott Kirby are both suddenly dropping Singapore Airlines and Emirates in interviews, Qantas is retiring the A380 early, and Frontier's elite program gets stripped for parts. Grab a beer, this one's got some good absurdity in it.

item.title: Runway Briefing — United's Rough Day, Kirby's Chicago Prediction, and Frontier Plays Both Sides
item.description: A United flight from LA to Newark turns into a two-stop odyssey after an engine issue forces a diversion to Vegas. United's CEO doubles down on his prediction that American will eventually bail on Chicago. Frontier makes Diamond status easier to reach while quietly gutting everyone else's perks. Plus, Boeing's engineers just said "no thanks" to the latest contract, and two air traffic controllers are getting fired over the LaGuardia crash.
